title: Custom Authorization Handlers
description: Build custom authorization handlers for complex business rules that go beyond built-in role and claim checks.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Custom Authorization Handlers**. Build custom authorization handlers for complex business rules that go beyond built-in role and claim checks. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Custom Authorization Handlers and be confident in applying it to your projects.
When to Build a Custom Handler

data.title: Common Use Cases
items: Time-based access (business hours only, feature flags with expiration)
Geolocation restrictions (access from approved countries only)
License validation (active subscription required for features)
Approval workflows (document requires manager approval before editing)
Quota enforcement (user has exceeded API call limit)
Combination rules (seniority + department + project assignment)

data.text: Handler Architecture

Every custom handler inherits from `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement>`. The framework calls `HandleRequirementAsync` for each registered requirement. Inside, you have access to the `AuthorizationHandlerContext` (which contains the user) and the requirement instance. You can inject any service you need via constructor DI.

data.title: Business Hours Authorization Handler

data.text: Combining Multiple Handlers

A single policy can have multiple requirements, each with its own handler. The authorization system evaluates all of them. This enables complex rules while keeping each piece of logic isolated and testable.

data.title: Complex Policy with Multiple Handlers
Handlers Must Be Thread-Safe
data.text: Authorization handlers may be called concurrently for the same request or across multiple requests. Avoid storing state in instance fields. Use scoped services only for the lifetime of a single authorization operation.
Testing Custom Handlers

Handlers are plain classes with no framework dependencies beyond `AuthorizationHandlerContext`. This makes them easy to unit test. Create mock users, requirements, and resources, then verify the handler calls `Succeed` or not.

data.title: Unit Testing a Custom Handler

data.text: Authorization in Frontend: A Complementary Pattern

While handlers run server-side, you can mirror the authorization logic in React using a custom hook or HOC. This is not a security measure but improves UX by hiding UI elements before the API rejects the request.

data.title: Custom Authorization Hook in React
Client-Side Authorization is Not Security
data.text: React hooks and conditional rendering are UX patterns, not security boundaries. An attacker can call your API directly with crafted requests. Always enforce authorization server-side in handlers or middleware.
Advanced Patterns

data.title: Advanced Handler Techniques
items: **Async resource loading**: Fetch additional data inside handlers using injected services
**Caching handlers**: Use `IAuthorizationCacheProvider` to cache expensive authorization decisions
**Fallback handlers**: Use `FallbackPolicy` to apply authorization globally with exceptions
**Dynamic requirements**: Create requirements at runtime based on configuration or feature flags
**Audit logging**: Log authorization decisions in handlers for compliance and debugging

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Custom handlers implement complex business authorization rules
Requirements are simple data carriers; handlers contain the logic
Multiple handlers can be combined in a single policy
Handlers should be thread-safe and easily unit-testable
Frontend authorization is UX-only; always enforce server-side
data.takeaway: Custom handlers transform ASP.NET Core's authorization from a simple gatekeeper into a flexible, business-aware security layer.

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **Custom Authorization Handlers**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of Custom Authorization Handlers when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Custom Authorization Handlers**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Custom Authorization Handlers**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
